title: Operators & Expressions
subtitle: Arithmetic, comparison, logical, and string operators
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Data sitting in variables is useless without the ability to calculate, compare, and combine it.
whyItExists.solution: Operators let you do arithmetic (+ - * /), compare values (== != < > <= >=), apply logic (and or not), and build formatted strings (f-strings).
whyItExists.whenToUse: Constantly — operators are the foundation of every expression and condition in Python.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Avoid chained comparisons without parentheses for clarity. Use Decimal instead of float for financial calculations.

explainModes.beginner: Operators are symbols that do things with values. + adds numbers (2 + 3 = 5) or joins strings ('Hello' + ' World'). == checks if two values are equal. and/or combine conditions. f-strings let you put variables inside text: f'Hello {name}'.
explainModes.simple: Arithmetic: + - * / // (floor div) % (modulo) ** (power). Comparison: == != < > <= >=. Logical: and, or, not. Assignment shortcuts: += -= *= /=. String: + (concat), * (repeat), f'{var}' (format). Membership: in, not in. Identity: is, is not.
explainModes.standard: Python operator precedence (high to low): ** → unary +/- → * / // % → + - → comparisons → not → and → or. Short-circuit evaluation: 'a and b' stops at a if a is False; 'a or b' stops at a if a is True. Augmented assignment (+=) modifies in place for mutable objects. Chained comparisons: 0 < x < 10 works naturally in Python.
explainModes.technical: Python operators are implemented as special (dunder) methods: + calls __add__, == calls __eq__, < calls __lt__. This enables operator overloading for custom classes. / always returns float (true division). // is floor division (returns int for int operands). @ operator (PEP 465) is for matrix multiplication (numpy). Bitwise operators: & | ^ ~ << >>.
explainModes.deepDive: Python's operator module provides functional equivalents (operator.add, operator.eq) useful for functional programming and sort keys. The := walrus operator (PEP 572) combines assignment and expression: while chunk := f.read(8192). is vs ==: is compares object identity (same memory address), == compares value — common bug: using is to compare strings (works by accident due to interning, not reliable).

content.code:
# Basic arithmetic
print(10 + 3)    # 13
print(10 - 3)    # 7
print(10 * 3)    # 30
print(10 / 3)    # 3.3333... (always float)
print(10 // 3)   # 3  (floor division — integer result)
print(10 % 3)    # 1  (modulo — remainder)
print(2 ** 10)   # 1024 (power)

# Order of operations
print(2 + 3 * 4)      # 14 (multiplication first)
print((2 + 3) * 4)    # 20 (brackets first)

# Augmented assignment
x = 10
x += 5   # x = x + 5  → 15
x *= 2   # x = x * 2  → 30
print(x) # 30

# Comparison — returns True or False
print(5 == 5)    # True
print(5 != 3)    # True
print(5 > 3)     # True
print(5 < 3)     # False
print(5 >= 5)    # True
print(5 <= 4)    # False

# Chained comparisons (unique to Python!)
age = 25
print(18 <= age < 65)  # True — works like math!

# Logical operators
print(True and True)   # True
print(True and False)  # False
print(True or False)   # True
print(not True)        # False

# Combining
x = 7
print(x > 0 and x < 10)   # True
print(x < 0 or x > 5)     # True
print(not (x == 7))        # False

name = 'Prashant'
age = 28
price = 9.99

# f-string: prefix with f, put expressions in {}
print(f'Hello, {name}!')
# → Hello, Prashant!

print(f'{name} is {age} years old')
# → Prashant is 28 years old

# Expressions inside {}
print(f'Next year: {age + 1}')
# → Next year: 29

# Format numbers
print(f'Price: ₹{price:.2f}')   # 2 decimal places
# → Price: ₹9.99

print(f'{1000000:,}')  # thousands separator
# → 1,000,000

# String operators
greeting = 'Hello' + ', ' + 'World!'   # concatenation
line = '-' * 20                         # repeat
print(greeting)   # Hello, World!
print(line)       # --------------------

questions.question: What is the result of 10 // 3 in Python?
questions.explanation: // is floor division — it divides and rounds DOWN to the nearest integer. 10 / 3 = 3.333..., floor of that is 3. Use % to get the remainder: 10 % 3 = 1.

faq.q: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3 in Python?
faq.a: Floating-point numbers use binary representation (IEEE 754), and 0.1 and 0.2 can't be represented exactly in binary — similar to how 1/3 can't be exactly represented in decimal. Use round(0.1 + 0.2, 1) == 0.3, or the decimal module for financial precision: from decimal import Decimal.

faq.q: What is the difference between == and is?
faq.a: == compares values (5 == 5.0 is True). is compares identity — whether two variables point to the exact same object in memory (a is b). Use == for value comparison. Use is only for None: if x is None: ...

examples: f-strings replaced .format() and % formatting — used in every modern Python codebase
// and % are essential for date/time arithmetic, pagination, and grid layouts
Chained comparisons (0 <= score < 100) are idiomatic Python — avoid JavaScript-style (score >= 0 && score < 100)
